candidates.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
candidates.content: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a Platonic Representation Theorem: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--good views--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with bad views, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated

candidates.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
candidates.content: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. candidates.title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss
candidates.content: Formula-Driven Supervised Learning (FDSL) enables vision pre-training without real images, but existing methods cast pre-training as classification on discretized labels, discarding continuity in the generative process. We propose Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning (FDSML), which derives relational supervision from image-generation parameters beyond discrete class labels. FDSML combines FineFractalDB, our refined fractal dataset with higher intra-class variation and more stable structures, with a Parameter-Aware Triplet (PA-Triplet) Loss that assigns positives and negatives according to distances in the underlying Iterated Function System parameter space. This objective trains embeddings to respect parameter-derived relative similarity orderings. Experiments show that FDSML improves transferability to image retrieval while remaining competitive on downstream classification and improving robustness under several corruption settings. On ResNet-50, Recall@1 improves from 65.6% to 74.0% on Stanford Online Products and from 56.2% to 78.4% on Stanford Cars over FDSL pre-training. candidates.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
candidates.content: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. candidates.content: [PHASE4] RECRUITING | 申办方/赞助方: Epicentre | 适应症: Ebola, Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD). The BRAVO study (Bundibugyo: Respondre Avec la Vaccination, "On est ensemble") was developed in response to the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The study focuses on frontline workers (FLWs), who are at increased risk of infection because of their involvement in patient care, outbreak response activities, and contact with affected communities. Protecting this population is critical for maintaining healthcare services and strengthening outbreak control efforts. Currently, there is no licensed vaccine specifically targeting Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) for broad use. However, ERVEBO®, a vaccine licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, is available and has demonstrated a favorable safety profile. Although preclinical and immunological evidence suggests that ERVEBO® may provide some degree of cross-protection against BDBV, the extent of protection remains uncertain. BRAVO therefore aims both to support rapid vaccination of frontline workers during the outbreak and to generate evidence that can inform future vaccine policy and preparedness strategies. BR

candidates.title: Blood Pressure Targets in Critically Ill Children
candidates.content: “Do I need to treat this blood pressure?” is one of the most common questions to pass through the minds of acute care pediatricians during a typical day in the hospital. Blood pressure generally increases with somatic growth, reflecting developmental changes in stroke volume, vascular structure and function, and neurohumoral regulation. As a result of interindividual variation across the developmental stages of childhood, there is a wide range of acceptable blood pressure values. There is also long-standing ambiguity about what should be considered the limits of acceptable blood pressure, particularly among hospitalized children. Age-based reference values offer a starting point, although the threshold used to identify an unusually low blood pressure may differ from the pressure needed to maintain adequate organ perfusion. This uncertainty can create substantial tension when a clinician faces the decision whether to manage potentially low blood pressure in a child. Treatments for potentially low blood pressure can also vary widely, from temporary stimulation to administration of vasopressor and inotropic medications through a central vascular catheter. candidates.title: Fixed Pupils: Neurologic Finality vs Poetic Repair
candidates.content: In “Holding Hope,” the poem’s crux is not simply the devastating neurologic sign of “fixed pupils,” but also the way this medical phrase is transformed in the ear of the shocked sibling of a mortally wounded patient into the impossible mercy of healing: “[t]hey fixed his pupils.” The clinical distancing inherent in a bedside case presentation, reflexively performed before a disbelieving family member, is translated by a kind of poetic mishearing from incomprehensible loss into hopeful repair. The patient’s sibling seems to only grasp fragments of reality, while the physicians only offer partial truths. Even the clinician-speaker of the poem struggles with what can be held medically vs emotionally, the gasping lines and broken-up stanzas structurally reflecting the patient’s wounded brain and body and the heartbreak of both family member and physician. Yet poetry here does not really restore hope like some kind of harmless magic bullet, nor does it heal the lethal real-world gunshot wounds; more painfully, perhaps, it tries to reconcile brutal finality with the disconsolate wish it were not so. candidates.title: [Series] Men's health: an intersectional and multilevel framework for understanding syndemic patterns of health
candidates.content: Men occupy a privileged position within gender power relations: the male body has been the default reference point for biomedical research and therapeutic development (with the historical exclusion of women from medical trials), and men dominate health services leadership and exercise well documented medical misogyny. Yet despite their privileged position, many aspects of men's health outcomes are neglected and undertheorised because they are not examined through an intersectional gender lens. Although consideration of gender and masculinity is important for understanding men's health, research thus far has focused predominantly on men's harmful health behaviours, overemphasising individual determinants of health, and a deficit-based approach.

candidates.title: [Perspectives] Aid cuts and the slow death of a rural lifeline
candidates.content: On my tenth visit, it took me two attempts to find the care and treatment centre (CTC) for people living with HIV/AIDS in Miono, Tanzania. The one-storey white building, where patients used to sit along wooden benches waiting to be called, was now filled with motorbikes and a few people milling outside doctors’ offices off to the side. There used to be two buildings in the complex, one for people living with HIV/AIDS and another a maternity clinic, both full of people and babies. Now there are six buildings and fewer patients, no boda bodas (motorcycle taxis) hanging around for a fare, or family members waiting in the shaded area outside.

candidates.title: Granzyme K-expressing CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells, complement activation and histotoxic immunity
candidates.content: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01364-5 This Perspective discusses the emerging biology of a unique population of granzyme K-expressing CD8+ T cells. Unlike canonical cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, which mediate direct cell killing, granzyme K-expressing CD8+ T cells activate the complement cascade and promote localized tissue inflammation. The authors propose that such ‘tissue histotoxicity’ is an important defence strategy, allowing CD8+ T cells to target a tissue neighbourhood instead of one cell at a time.

candidates.title: [Viewpoint] Reframing the manosphere: a public health response to a commercial ecosystem
candidates.content: The manosphere, a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny, and male victimisation, is an under-recognised determinant of health harms. This network has been implicated in considerable health harms: widespread mental health impacts, especially in young people; violence against women, girls, and gender minorities; and delegitimising help-seeking in boys and men. In this Viewpoint, we argue that the manosphere is best understood and addressed as a public health problem.

candidates.title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington’s disease cortical and striatal neurons
candidates.content: Single-cell-resolution analysis of brain tissue in Huntington's disease (HD) reveals that cortical and striatal neurons pass through analogous biological changes, each initiated by a neuron's own expanding DNA repeat. In cortical neurons, as in striatal neurons, the DNA repeat expands somatically over decades (phases A and B) and becomes toxic at about 150 CAGs, initiating cell-identity erosion (phase C), the formation of nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein, a derepression crisis (phase D), and then death of the neuron.

candidates.title: Region-specific generation and retention of acetylated cohesin shape the genome-wide pattern of sister chromatid cohesion
candidates.content: Abstract Sister chromatid cohesion depends on ESCO2-mediated acetylation of the cohesin subunit SMC3, yet how this modification is established and maintained across the genome remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the chromatin-binding dynamics of ESCO2 and its enzymatic activity using quantitative ChIP-seq of human cells synchronously progressing through S phase. ESCO2 bound broadly along chromosomes without forming discrete peaks and preferentially localized to transcriptionally inactive regions, but was not confined to H3K9me3- or H3K27me3-enriched heterochromatin. Consistent with this binding pattern, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation showed a similarly broad distribution in these regions. In contrast, ESCO1, a paralog of ESCO2, primarily mediated SMC3 acetylation at cohesin peak sites. Notably, most of the broadly distributed, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation generated during S phase was progressively lost from chromatin after replication, whereas the fraction that persisted into late G2 accumulated in domains enriched for the repressive H3K27me3 modification. candidates.title: Queuosine-modification dependent histidyl tRNA fragment promotes cell-type dependent proliferation
candidates.content: Abstract tRNA fragments (tRFs) are natural, small non-coding RNAs produced by endogenous ribonucleolytic cleavage of tRNAs. tRFs play a role in many biological pathways, including regulation of cell proliferation. Specific tRNA modifications affect tRF biogenesis. Queuosine (Q) modification occurs at the wobble anticodon nucleotide of 4 mammalian tRNAs and protects these tRNAs from fragmentation. Here, we investigated cell-type and tRNA Q-modification dependencies on mammalian cell proliferation. We found that Q-modified tRNA can either increase, decrease, or make no difference in proliferation. Proliferation decreased in MCF7, a breast cancer cell line, when tRNAs were Q-modified and dependent on the modification enzyme complex, QTRT1/2. MCF7 proliferation increases upon the transfection of Q-modification-dependent tRF His or decreases upon knockdown of endogenous tRF His . Consistent with Q-dependent proliferation reduction, polysome profiling showed decreased translation efficiency of ribosomal proteins. candidates.title: Dynamic phosphorylation of TCOF1 controlled by CK2 and PPM1D regulates nucleolar condensation and RNA polymerase I activity
candidates.content: Abstract The nucleolus is a membrane-less organelle essential for ribosomal DNA (rDNA) transcription and ribosome biogenesis, yet the mechanisms regulating its dynamic assembly remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the phosphatase protein phosphatase magnesium-dependent 1 delta (PPM1D) as a key regulator of the nucleolar architecture via dephosphorylation of the scaffold protein TCOF1. By combining super-resolution microscopy and domain mapping, we show that PPM1D localizes to the nucleolus through a conserved motif at the C-terminus. Phosphoproteomic analysis and structural modeling revealed that PPM1D targets casein kinase 2 (CK2)-phosphorylated sites within the low-complexity repeat domain of TCOF1, which impacts its interaction with RNA polymerase I (Pol I), immobilization in the fibrillar centres, and nucleolar condensation. Disruption of the phosphorylation balance by loss of PPM1D or inhibition of CK2 leads to nucleolar disorganization and reduced rDNA transcription. Finally, we demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of PPM1D sensitizes cells to RNA Pol I inhibitors, in both p53-dependent and -independent contexts. candidates.title: Engineered probiotics target granulomas to treat mycobacterial infection
candidates.content: Granulomas are a pathological niche for mycobacteria that remain difficult to access with conventional therapies. Here we show that probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) infiltrates and colonizes granulomas and can be engineered as a delivery system that senses the local microenvironment and releases antimycobacterial payloads. Specifically, we leveraged the hypoxic microenvironment of necrotic granulomas to restrict bacterial growth, and developed a dual-mode lysis circuit combining intracellular and extracellular killing for sustained payload release with limited evolutionary escape. We further engineered EcN to express a mycobacteriophage-derived enzyme, generating a strain that suppressed drug-sensitive and drug-resistant mycobacteria in vitro and potentiated conventional antibiotic activity. Engineered probiotics also reduced mycobacterial burden in vivo, and in a murine model of rifampicin-resistant infection, combination treatment with pretomanid achieved greater bacterial reduction than either monotherapy. Together, these results establish a synthetic biology framework for targeting granulomatous infections with programmable living microbes.

candidates.title: Expanding the therapeutic window of bacteria for cancer therapy
candidates.content: Engineered bacteria enable self-amplifying therapeutic delivery and immune activation, yet these same features drive systemic toxicity and off-target growth. Here, we create a "tumorobe" that overcomes these limitations by integrating reduced immunogenicity, tumour-restricted growth, and enhanced payload release. Specifically, we identify lipopolysaccharide modifications that reduce immunogenicity while preserving fitness, restrict growth to tumours using a hypoxia-lactate "AND" gate, and enhance extracellular payload release via lipoprotein deletion. This strain expands the maximum tolerated dose in a route-dependent manner by up to 1,000-fold. Across multiple murine models, including colorectal cancer and glioblastoma, the strain drives robust antitumour efficacy as both a standalone therapeutic and an immunotherapeutic delivery platform, achieving durable complete responses in up to 75% of colorectal tumours when armed with a cytokine payload. Together, these results establish a broadly applicable platform for safe and effective bacterial cancer therapy.

candidates.title: A Synthetic Virology Platform for Rapid Prototyping of Influenza A Virus mutants
candidates.content: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a significant public health threat, with the need for effective vaccines and antiviral therapies remaining a high priority. In vitro testing is paramount in studying novel IAV viruses and their immunogenicity. To address this need, we developed a synthetic virology approach to rapidly prototype and test IAV mutants with altered antigenic sites. By strategically inserting restriction sites within an ambisense plasmid, we generated a tool where we can seamlessly replace either 1) the full hemagglutinin (HA), 2) the HA globular head domain to generate head/stalk chimeras or 3) the five canonical antigenic sites. The cloning inserts can be computationally designed and artificially synthesized, enabling rescue of synthetic Influenza A viruses. Using this platform we rescued IAV H1N1, H3N2 & H5N1, and went on to prototype their respective antigenic site mutants & chimeric IAVs using viral genome sequence alone. This platform could be useful for generating vaccine seed strains or to study anti-viral immunity.

candidates.title: Reinforcement learning to improve large language model-based automated code compliance systems
candidates.content: arXiv:2606.22402v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based approaches for automated code compliance (ACC) of building regulations are prone to generating incorrect and hallucinated computer-processable rules. This paper introduces P4IR, a two-stage framework that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to instill domain knowledge in an LLM, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve the accuracy of the generated intermediate representations in the form of high-level code skeletons. The framework achieved final reductions of up to 21.3% and 41.0% in tree edit distance and token-level Levenshtein distance respectively, relative to the SFT baselines. Comparative analysis demonstrates that this approach in a zero-shot setting outperforms leading LLMs in both code structure and semantics, evaluated via few-shot prompting. Additionally, the GRPO stage produced a statistically significant reduction in false positives. By combining SFT with GRPO to optimize directly for domain-specific objectives, this approach offers a path toward more accurate and reliable LLM-based ACC systems.

candidates.title: Robust Instruction Compliance in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
candidates.content: arXiv:2605.12655v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in real-world use cases may need to adapt to external natural language instructions that interrupt ongoing behavior and conflict with long-horizon objectives. However, conditioning rewards on instructions introduces a fundamental failure mode as Bellman updates couple value estimates across instruction contexts, leading to inconsistent values when instructions interrupt macro-actions. We propose Macro-Action Value Correction for Instruction Compliance (MAVIC), which corrects Bellman backups at instruction boundaries by correcting the incoming instruction objective and restoring the continuation value under the current objective. Unlike reward shaping, MAVIC modifies the bootstrapping target itself, enabling consistent value estimation under stochastic instruction switching within a unified policy. We provide theoretical analysis and an actor-critic implementation, and show that MAVIC achieves high instruction compliance while preserving base task performance in increasingly complex cooperative multi-agent environments.

candidates.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
candidates.content: arXiv:2610.40030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
